title: Reading stack traces

overview.what:
A stack trace is a detailed error report that Python prints when your code crashes. It shows the exact path the code took before it failed.

Imagine tracking a package delivery. The history shows exactly which cities the package passed through before it got lost. A stack trace shows exactly which functions your code called before the error happened.

```python
def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

def calculate_marks(total):
    # The error actually happens inside divide(),
    # but we called it from here.
    return divide(total, 0)

calculate_marks(100)
```

The rule is: **read a stack trace from the bottom up.** The very last line tells you the exact error (e.g., `ZeroDivisionError`). The lines immediately above it tell you exactly which file and line number caused it.
overview.why: It tells you exactly where to look to fix a crash. Without a stack trace, you would have to guess which function failed.

why_learning_this: You will stop panicking when you see a massive block of red error text.
You will instantly know which line of code to fix.

common_mistakes.title: Reading from the top
common_mistakes.explanation: You start reading the top of the stack trace and get confused by deep library files. The actual error name and your specific code are usually at the bottom.

common_mistakes.title: Ignoring the error type
common_mistakes.explanation: You stare at the line numbers but don't read the very last line. The last line (like `TypeError: expected str`) tells you exactly what you did wrong.

recall_questions.q: Explain what a stack trace is in your own words, as if to a classmate.
recall_questions.answer: It is an error report that shows the path your code took before it crashed, highlighting the exact functions and line numbers involved.

recall_questions.q: In which direction should you read a Python stack trace?
recall_questions.answer: You should read it from the bottom up. The bottom line tells you the exact error that occurred.

understanding_checks.question: A stack trace shows an error happening inside `fastapi/routing.py`. Should you go edit `fastapi/routing.py` to fix the bug?
understanding_checks.answer: No. You should look slightly higher in the stack trace for a file that YOU wrote. You probably passed bad data to FastAPI.
understanding_checks.why: Read a stack trace from the bottom up. The error often happens inside a library because your code gave it invalid data. Fix your code, not the library.

understanding_checks.question: Your code crashes and prints 50 lines of error text. A classmate says, 'This is a huge error, your whole app is broken.' Is this true?
understanding_checks.answer: No. A long stack trace just means the code passed through many functions before the single failure occurred.
understanding_checks.why: The length of the stack trace only shows how deeply nested the function calls were. It does not mean the error is hard to fix.

aha_moment.prediction: If `c()` crashes, will the stack trace mention `a()`?
aha_moment.common_guess: No, because the crash is in c().
aha_moment.why: The stack trace shows the full path. It will show `a()` called `b()`, and `b()` called `c()`. This helps you trace the origin of the bad data.

challenge.title: Trigger an error chain
challenge.prompt: Write two functions. `first()` should call `second()`. `second()` should trigger a `ZeroDivisionError` by dividing 1 by 0. Call `first()`.
